title: Dice v. Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Co. (1952)
summary: The state court could not use its own restrictive fraud and decision-maker rules to defeat the employee’s federal railway claim.
notes:
Do not restate this as general incorporation of the Seventh Amendment against the states. The reasoning concerns the federal statutory right and its enforcement. It also provides a carefully bounded connection to Contracts release and misrepresentation doctrines.

Dice, a railroad fireman, alleged the railroad told him the release was merely a receipt for back pay; the trial court entered judgment notwithstanding the jury's verdict, the Ohio Court of Appeals reversed, the Ohio Supreme Court reinstated judgment for the railroad, and the U.S. Supreme Court (Black, J.) reversed.

Justice Frankfurter's separate opinion, joined by Justices Reed, Jackson and Burton, concurred in reversal on the release question but dissented from requiring the state court to send the fraud issue to the jury.

sections.Parties: Dice, an injured railroad employee, sued his employer under the Federal Employers’ Liability Act.
sections.Material Facts: Dice signed a document after receiving money that he understood to represent payments connected to his injury. He claimed the railroad misrepresented the document, which purported to release his claim. Under the Ohio approach, failure to read could defeat his fraud challenge and the judge could decide the issue. Federal law protected the FELA claim against a release procured by the alleged misrepresentation and assigned an important role to the jury.
sections.Procedural History: A jury returned a verdict for Dice, but the state court displaced that result under the state approach. The Supreme Court reversed, requiring the federal treatment of the release and jury issue.
sections.Issue: Could a state court applying FELA use state rules that impaired the federal protection against a fraudulent release and removed the issue from the jury?
sections.Holding: No. Federal law governed the release’s validity and protected jury determination in the circumstances presented.
sections.Reasoning: A federal right does not lose its essential protections when Congress permits enforcement in state court. The Court considered uniform federal treatment of FELA releases important to the statutory protection, and regarded the jury’s role as a substantial part of that protection. State rules describing a signer as negligent for failing to read could not override the federal treatment of the alleged fraud. The case therefore differs from Erie’s usual direction: here a state tribunal was enforcing a federally created right.

learning.why: The state court could not use its own restrictive fraud and decision-maker rules to defeat the employee’s federal railway claim.

topics.cp-reverse-erie: State courts enforcing a federal claim had to respect the federal rules protecting that claim.
topics.cp-judge-jury: The jury’s role was treated as integral to the federal FELA right in this setting.
topics.cp-release: The validity of the allegedly fraudulently obtained release was governed by federal law.
topics.cp-federalism: The case tests how far a state court hearing a federal claim must yield its own procedural allocation to federal law.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Frankfurter and other dissenters agreed that federal law controlled the release’s validity but disputed the need to impose the federal judge-jury allocation on the state court.

mnemonic.rationale: A release the fireman was told was a receipt
